problem:
The rate at which the number of particles in a radioactive substance decays $N(t),$ after $t$ years, can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}=-0.01N.
$$

How many years will it take for the number of particles to be $1%$ of the original number? Round your answer to the nearest year.
worked_solution:
We model the number of particles using the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}=-0.01N.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
N(t)={N}_{0}\,{e}^{-0.01t},
$$

where ${N}_{0}$ is the initial number of particles.

Let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the number of particles is $1%$ of its initial number. That is,

$$
N({t}_{1})=0.01{N}_{0}.
$$

We solve the above equation for ${t}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.01{N}_{0} & ={N}_{0}\,{e}^{-0.01{t}_{1}} \\ 0.01 & ={e}^{-0.01{t}_{1}} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.01) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-0.01{t}_{1}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.01) & =-0.01{t}_{1} \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.01)}{0.01} \\ {t}_{1} & ≈460.517\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we conclude that it takes $461$ years for the number of particles to be $1%$ of the original number.
